body.statement:
For every member of \(\mathfrak M\), there is a continuous function \(a:\mathcal K\to(0,\infty)\) such that
\[
\sup_{\beta\in\mathcal K}
\left|n\,d_{T_n^{\mathrm{full}}}(\beta)-a(\beta)\right|\longrightarrow0.
\]
For every sequence of uniformly sampled balanced complements \(T_{n,m}^{\mathrm{main}}\) with \(N=n-m\to\infty\),
\[
E_{S_m}\sup_{\beta\in\mathcal K}
\left|N\,d_{T_{n,m}^{\mathrm{main}}}(\beta)-a(\beta)\right|\longrightarrow0.
\]
With \(\mathcal B_\infty(\beta)=\lim_n\mathcal B_{T_n^{\mathrm{full}}}(\beta)\), \(M_\beta=\mathcal B_\infty(\beta)^{\mathsf T}W\mathcal B_\infty(\beta)\), \(g_\beta(z)=z^{\mathsf T}G_\infty(\beta)z\), and \(Z\sim N(0,I_{Fp})\), the coefficient is
\[
a(\beta)
=(1-\eta)\operatorname{tr}(M_\beta)
\left[
E\{g_\beta(Z)\}
-\alpha^{-1}E\!\left\{g_\beta(Z)
\mathbf 1\!\left(g_\beta(Z)\leq q_{\alpha,\beta}\right)\right\}
\right].
\]
Moreover,
\[
0<\inf_{\beta\in\mathcal K}a(\beta)
\leq\sup_{\beta\in\mathcal K}a(\beta)<\infty.
\]
For every balanced pilot-size sequence \(m=m(n)\in\mathcal M_n\) with \(N\to\infty\), the exact deletion contrast satisfies
\[
\sup_{\beta\in\mathcal K}
\left|nD_{n,m}(\beta)-\frac mn a(\beta)\right|
\longrightarrow0.
\]
Consequently, if \(m/n\to c\in[0,1]\), then, uniformly in \(\beta\),
\[
n\left[
d_{T_n^{\mathrm{full}}}(\beta)
-\left(\frac{N}{n}\right)^2
E_{S_m}d_{T_{n,m}^{\mathrm{main}}}(\beta)
\right]\longrightarrow c\,a(\beta).
\]
These first-order relations do not assert the sharper deletion expansion on the scale \(m/n^2+(nm)^{-1}\) when \(m/n\to0\).
body.justification: The theorem gives the first-order exact-mixture gain and the uniform exact deletion relation for every diverging main wave.
body.gap: It does not identify the candidate coefficient \(A\) on the square-root pilot scale.
body.consumer: It quantifies macroscopic deletion and supplies the deletion lower bound used in both branches of the endpoint lemma.
body.proof_tex:
Fix a member of \(\mathfrak M\) and condition throughout on its deterministic complete baseline array.  Put
\[
w_q=2^{1-K_f}c_q,
\qquad
\mu_{iq}(\beta)=E_\beta\{Y_{in}(q)\mid x_{in}\},
\qquad
\varepsilon_{iq}=Y_{in}(q)-\mu_{iq}(\beta).
\tag{1}
\]
The functions in (1), together with their \(\rho\)-derivatives through order three, are continuous and uniformly bounded on \(\mathcal X\times\mathcal K\) by \(\mathrm{ass{:}arraywise\text{-}moment\text{-}regularity}\).  The empirical baseline measures converge by \(\mathrm{ass{:}baseline\text{-}limit}\), and \(\mathrm{ass{:}baseline\text{-}gram}\) keeps the imbalance covariance nonsingular on its effective range.  Applying these facts to the empirical covariances that define \(\mathcal B_T(\beta)\), and using constant rank from \(\mathrm{ass{:}oracle\text{-}rank}\), gives, uniformly in \(\beta\),
\[
\mathcal B_{T_n^{\mathrm{full}}}(\beta)
\longrightarrow \mathcal B_\infty(\beta).
\tag{2}
\]
Indeed, on a fixed-rank stratum the Moore--Penrose inverse is continuous: writing a singular-value decomposition with the positive singular values bounded away from zero by \(\mathrm{ass{:}baseline\text{-}gram}\), inversion of those singular values is continuous and the zero singular values remain zero.  The same sampling-without-replacement variance calculation, applied to each uniformly bounded moment function, yields (2) in probability for a uniformly sampled complement of size \(N\to\infty\).  The normalization in the definition of \(G_T\), together with \(\mathrm{lem{:}experiment\text{-}indexed\text{-}oracle\text{-}convergence}\), identifies
\[
G_\infty(\beta)=\frac{M_\beta}{\operatorname{tr}(M_\beta)},
\qquad
M_\beta=\mathcal B_\infty(\beta)^{\mathsf T}W\mathcal B_\infty(\beta).
\tag{3}
\]
The denominator in (3) is bounded away from zero uniformly in \(\beta\): this follows from \(\mathrm{ass{:}full\text{-}oracle\text{-}signal\text{-}floor}\) and (2).  Uniform moment boundedness also gives a finite uniform upper bound.

For a balanced set \(T\) of size \(k\), define the ordinary cell-contrast statistic
\[
\widetilde{\boldsymbol\tau}_T
=\frac1k\sum_{i\in T}\sum_{q\in\mathcal Q}
Qw_q\mathbf 1\{Z_i=q\}Y_{in}(q).
\tag{4}
\]
Under balanced complete randomization \(P(Z_i=q)=1/Q\), so (4) is its exact Horvitz--Thompson estimator.  Apply \(\mathrm{lem{:}balanced\text{-}random\text{-}partition\text{-}clt}\) to the bounded deterministic vector consisting of all conditional means in (1) and the baseline coordinates.  Its negligible-maximum-influence condition follows from \(\mathrm{ass{:}baseline\text{-}bound}\) and the uniform bound on \(\mu_{iq}\).  After standardizing the nondegenerate imbalance coordinates, the lemma gives jointly
\[
\left(
\sqrt{k}\{\widetilde{\boldsymbol\tau}^{\,\mu}_T
-\boldsymbol\tau_T^\mu\},
\sqrt{k}\Delta_T
\right)
\Rightarrow
\left(\mathcal B_\infty(\beta)Z+R,Z\right),
\tag{5}
\]
where \(Z\sim N(0,I_{Fp})\), \(R\) is centered Gaussian, and \(\operatorname{Cov}(R,Z)=0\).  Joint Gaussianity therefore makes \(R\) independent of \(Z\).  This is a random-partition limit for the deterministic conditional-mean table, not an assertion that the outcome residuals are Gaussian.

Under \(p_{T,H}\), the Radon--Nikodym derivative relative to balanced complete randomization is
\[
\eta+\frac{1-\eta}{\alpha}a_{T,H},
\tag{6}
\]
which lies between \(\eta\) and \(\eta+(1-\eta)/\alpha\) by \(\mathrm{def{:}exact\text{-}mixture}\).  Take \(H=G_T(\beta)\), which is admissible by \(\mathrm{lem{:}oracle\text{-}action\text{-}admissible}\).  By \(\mathrm{lem{:}experiment\text{-}indexed\text{-}oracle\text{-}convergence}\), the standardized quadratic score converges to \(g_\beta(Z)\).  By \(\mathrm{lem{:}gaussian\text{-}boundary\text{-}regularity}\), \(g_\beta(Z)\) has no mass at \(q_{\alpha,\beta}\).  Hence the randomized finite tie boundary has vanishing limiting mass, and the factor in (6) converges in \(L_1\) to
\[
\eta+\frac{1-\eta}{\alpha}
\mathbf 1\{g_\beta(Z)\leq q_{\alpha,\beta}\}.
\tag{7}
\]
The exact randomization second-moment identity in \(\mathrm{lem{:}balanced\text{-}random\text{-}partition\text{-}clt}\) gives convergence of the second moments in (5).  Since (6) is uniformly bounded, those quadratic terms remain uniformly integrable after tilting.

The independent residual \(R\) has the same quadratic contribution before and after the tilt in (7), because the tilt is measurable with respect to \(Z\).  The imbalance-explained contribution is
\[
Z^{\mathsf T}M_\beta Z
=\operatorname{tr}(M_\beta)g_\beta(Z).
\tag{8}
\]
Consequently, if \(V_T^\mu\) denotes the design risk with the potential-outcome table replaced by its conditional-mean table, (5)--(8) give
\[
\begin{aligned}
&k\{V_T^\mu(0,\beta)-V_T^\mu(G_T(\beta),\beta)\}\\
&\quad\longrightarrow
(1-\eta)\operatorname{tr}(M_\beta)
\left[
E\{g_\beta(Z)\}
-\alpha^{-1}E\!\left\{
g_\beta(Z)\mathbf 1(g_\beta(Z)\leq q_{\alpha,\beta})
\right\}
\right]
=a(\beta).
\end{aligned}
\tag{9}
\]

We now verify that exact unequal inclusions and outcome residuals do not change (9).  The exact mixture formula gives
\[
\pi_{iq}(T,G_T)
=\frac1Q\left[
\eta+\frac{1-\eta}{\alpha}
E_{\mathrm{CR}}\{a_{T,G_T}\mid Z_i=q\}
\right].
\tag{10}
\]
Conditioning on \(Z_i=q\) removes one bounded unit from the remaining random partition and shifts standardized imbalance by \(O(k^{-1/2})\), uniformly in \(i\).  Apply \(\mathrm{lem{:}balanced\text{-}random\text{-}partition\text{-}clt}\) to the remaining units.  The zero boundary mass used in (7) then gives
\[
\sup_{\beta\in\mathcal K}\max_{i\in T,q\in\mathcal Q}
\left|
E_{\mathrm{CR}}\{a_{T,G_T}\mid Z_i=q\}-\alpha
\right|\longrightarrow0.
\tag{11}
\]
To justify the displayed uniformity, suppose it failed.  A failing sequence admits a convergent parameter subsequence by compactness of \(\mathcal K\); bounded moment equicontinuity and (2) reduce that subsequence to the pointwise leave-one-unit limit, contradicting the Gaussian zero-boundary-mass conclusion.  Equations (10)--(11) imply
\[
\sup_{\beta\in\mathcal K}\max_{i,q}
\left|\pi_{iq}(T,G_T)-\frac1Q\right|\longrightarrow0.
\tag{12}
\]
The same joint limit, together with symmetry of the centered Gaussian quadratic lower tail, shows that (4) has bias \(o(k^{-1/2})\) under the tilt (6).  The balanced identities \(\sum_{i\in T}\pi_{iq}=k/Q\), (12), and the exact second-moment bound in \(\mathrm{lem{:}uniform\text{-}single\text{-}wave\text{-}risk}\) then imply
\[
\sqrt{k}\left(
\widehat{\boldsymbol\tau}^{\mathrm{HT}}_T(G_T)
-\widetilde{\boldsymbol\tau}_T
\right)\longrightarrow0
\quad\text{in }L_2.
\tag{13}
\]
Thus inverse-inclusion weighting adds no conditional-mean contribution to (9).

For the residual calculation, put
\(\sigma_{i,qr}(\beta)=E_\beta(\varepsilon_{iq}\varepsilon_{ir}\mid x_{in})\).  Independence across units under \(\mathrm{ass{:}stable\text{-}product\text{-}law}\) removes every term with distinct unit indices.  For the same unit and \(q\ne r\),
\[
E\left[
\left\{\frac{\mathbf 1(Z_i=q)}{\pi_{iq}}-1\right\}
\left\{\frac{\mathbf 1(Z_i=r)}{\pi_{ir}}-1\right\}
\right]=-1,
\tag{14}
\]
because one unit cannot receive two labels.  Thus the cross-treatment, same-unit terms cancel exactly when complete randomization is compared with the mixture.  The diagonal difference is
\[
\frac1{k^2}\sum_{i\in T}\sum_{q\in\mathcal Q}
w_q^{\mathsf T}Ww_q\,\sigma_{i,qq}(\beta)
\left(Q-\frac1{\pi_{iq}(T,G_T)}\right).
\tag{15}
\]
The conditional variances are uniformly bounded by \(\mathrm{ass{:}arraywise\text{-}moment\text{-}regularity}\).  Multiplying (15) by \(k\) and using (12) makes it converge uniformly to zero.  Since the conditional-mean and residual cross term has conditional expectation zero, (9), (13), and (15) prove
\[
\sup_{\beta\in\mathcal K}
\left|k\,d_T(\beta)-a(\beta)\right|\longrightarrow0
\tag{16}
\]
along the full array.

For a uniform random complement with \(N\to\infty\), sampling-without-replacement variances of the bounded moment functions are \(O(N^{-1})\), so the same argument yields (16) in probability over the split.  Moreover, for this fixed model member, the common conditional second-moment envelope and \(\mathrm{lem{:}uniform\text{-}single\text{-}wave\text{-}risk}\) give a constant \(C<\infty\) such that
\[
N|d_T(\beta)|
\leq N\{V_T(0,\beta)+V_T(G_T(\beta),\beta)\}
\leq C
\tag{17}
\]
uniformly in \(\beta\) and in balanced complements.  The domination in (17) upgrades convergence in probability to
\[
E_{S_m}\sup_{\beta\in\mathcal K}
\left|N d_T(\beta)-a(\beta)\right|\longrightarrow0.
\tag{18}
\]

Continuity of \(a\) follows from (2)--(3), \(\mathrm{lem{:}gaussian\text{-}boundary\text{-}regularity}\), and dominated convergence.  By \(\mathrm{ass{:}oracle\text{-}rank}\), \(G_\infty(\beta)\) has positive rank, while (3) gives trace one.  Thus \(g_\beta(Z)\) is nonnegative and nonconstant.  Because \(0<\alpha<1\) and its boundary distribution is atomless,
\[
\alpha^{-1}E\!\left[
g_\beta(Z)\mathbf 1\{g_\beta(Z)\leq q_{\alpha,\beta}\}
\right]
<E\{g_\beta(Z)\}.
\tag{19}
\]
The signal floor, \(0<\eta<1\), compactness of \(\mathcal K\), continuity, and (19) prove
\[
0<\inf_{\beta\in\mathcal K}a(\beta)
\leq\sup_{\beta\in\mathcal K}a(\beta)<\infty.
\tag{20}
\]

It remains to expose the stronger deletion relation.  For every balanced sequence with \(N\to\infty\), define
\[
u_n=\sup_{\beta\in\mathcal K}
\left|n d_{T_n^{\mathrm{full}}}(\beta)-a(\beta)\right|,
\qquad
v_n=E_{S_m}\sup_{\beta\in\mathcal K}
\left|N d_{T_{n,m}^{\mathrm{main}}}(\beta)-a(\beta)\right|.
\tag{21}
\]
Equations (16) and (18) give \(u_n\to0\) and \(v_n\to0\).  From \(\mathrm{def{:}exact\text{-}risk\text{-}components}\) and \(N=n-m\),
\[
\begin{aligned}
nD_{n,m}(\beta)-\frac mn a(\beta)
&=n d_{T_n^{\mathrm{full}}}(\beta)-a(\beta)\\
&\quad-\frac Nn E_{S_m}
\left\{N d_{T_{n,m}^{\mathrm{main}}}(\beta)-a(\beta)\right\}.
\end{aligned}
\tag{22}
\]
Therefore
\[
\sup_{\beta\in\mathcal K}
\left|nD_{n,m}(\beta)-\frac mn a(\beta)\right|
\leq u_n+\frac Nn v_n\longrightarrow0.
\tag{23}
\]
If \(m/n\to c<1\), then \(N\to\infty\), and (23) gives the asserted corollary.  If \(c=1\) while \(N\) stays bounded along a subsequence, (17) gives
\[
\frac Nn E_{S_m}\left|N d_{T_{n,m}^{\mathrm{main}}}(\beta)\right|
\leq \frac Nn C\longrightarrow0,
\tag{24}
\]
uniformly in \(\beta\); if \(N\to\infty\) along a subsequence, (23) applies.  Every subsequence has a further subsequence of one of these two kinds, so the \(c=1\) corollary follows as well.  Equation (23) is first order and does not control its remainder relative to \(m/n^2\) when \(m/n\to0\), which is why no frontier-scale coefficient is claimed.
